implementation_notes: std::function is a general-purpose polymorphic function wrapper that stores any CopyConstructible callable - function pointer, lambda, bind expression, function object - so the strategy interface collapses into one call signature and the context needs no base class at all. It is the lowest-friction runtime strategy vehicle: the caller passes a lambda, the type erasure keeps the context independent of it, and std::sort's comparator overload shows the same idea in the standard library. The classic abstract-base form (virtual-interface variant) remains the right choice when the strategy exposes several operations, must keep a stable ABI, or the call is hot enough that the extra indirection and a possible heap allocation matter.
pitfalls: std::function requires a copy-constructible target: a lambda capturing a std::unique_ptr or an ofstream does not compile (C++23's std::move_only_function is the fix).
The callable may exceed the small-buffer optimisation and allocate on assignment, so building a strategy inside a hot loop costs a heap allocation per iteration.
An empty std::function throws std::bad_function_call when invoked, so a context that accepts a default-constructed strategy must test operator bool first or install a default lambda.

variants.name: Abstract base class with virtual operation (classic GoF form)
variants.idiom_name: abstract Strategy base + Context holding Strategy* (unique_ptr/reference)
variants.implementation_notes: The canonical GoF shape in C++: an abstract base class with a pure virtual operation and a virtual destructor, one derived class per algorithm, and a context that owns the strategy through std::unique_ptr (or borrows it as a reference); std::sort's comparator overload takes the same idea as a template instead. Choose it when the strategy has several operations, when the boundary must stay ABI-stable behind a vtable, or when the algorithms are long-lived stateless singletons that can be shared. The cost is one virtual call and a possible pointer hop, removed only by devirtualisation or link-time optimisation.
pitfalls: The base needs a virtual destructor; deleting a concrete strategy through a base pointer without one is undefined behaviour.
Holding the strategy by value slices it (copy assignment through the base keeps only the base subobject), so hold a pointer or reference and delete the copy operations on polymorphic bases.
A virtual call in a hot loop blocks inlining unless the compiler devirtualises a monomorphic call site; measure before assuming the indirection is free.

variants.name: Template parameter policy (compile-time strategy, zero dispatch cost)
variants.implementation_notes: Move the choice from run time to compile time: parameterise the context with the algorithm (template<class Pricing = RetailPricing> class Checkout) so the compiler sees the concrete policy, inlines the call and emits no vtable - policy-based design, the idiom behind std::allocator and every comparator, hash and traits policy in the standard library. The interface contract is documented rather than enforced (a C++20 concepts-constrained policy checks it at instantiation time). The price is type-level: each policy combination is a distinct type, so a heterogeneous collection needs an extra type-erasure layer and the choice must be known when the context is instantiated.
pitfalls: Each policy combination is a distinct type: Checkout<A> and Checkout<B> cannot share one std::vector without type erasure, and the template parameter spreads to every type that holds the context.

A policy that carries state behaves like a strategy object; runtime polymorphism is then usually simpler, and the standard library's own hybrid is std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator (a compile-time policy dispatching at run time).
Without a concepts or static_assert contract the policy is duck-typed: a missing or differently named member is reported deep inside the context's body at instantiation time.
